question: I live in Calgary, far inland. In Canada's major ocean-drainage geography, why can my region still be described as part of the Hudson Bay watershed?
generated_answer:
The Hudson Bay watershed is much larger than just the immediate area around Hudson Bay itself. It includes a vast network of rivers and tributaries that drain into Hudson Bay. Even though Calgary is located far inland, it is part of the larger drainage system that eventually flows into Hudson Bay.

The Canadian Rockies, where Calgary is located, are part of the Continental Divide. Water on the western side of the Rockies flows into the Pacific Ocean via the Columbia River system, while water on the eastern side flows into the Hudson Bay watershed. The Bow and Red Deer rivers, which flow through or near Calgary, are part of this eastern drainage system. They eventually flow into the Saskatchewan River, which in turn flows into Lake Winnipeg, and then into Hudson Bay.

This means that, despite being far from Hudson Bay, Calgary is part of the larger Hudson Bay watershed because the water that flows through the region eventually makes its way to Hudson Bay.

This principle applies to many areas in Canada and the United States, where large watersheds cover vast regions and include many different rivers and drainage areas. Even if a location is far from a major body of water like Hudson Bay, it can still be part of the larger watershed if it is connected to the network of rivers and streams that eventually drain into that body of water. 

In summary, Calgary is part of the Hudson Bay watershed because it is connected to a network of rivers and streams that flow into Hudson Bay, even though it is located far inland.
